title: Terrain and Friction: Surfaces, Slopes, and What the Ground Lets a Vehicle Do

questions.question: What decides the most force a tyre can put on the ground?
options: The weight on it times the friction coefficient
questions.explanation: The ground pushes back with at most the load times the friction. Ask for more and the wheel slips.

questions.question: At 2 m/s, ice against tarmac made the stopping distance:
options: The same, since the brakes are the same
questions.explanation: 0.250 m on tarmac and 1.853 m on ice. The most a vehicle can brake is g times the friction plus the rolling resistance.

questions.question: Going down a grade of 0.2 on gravel, the stop from 2 m/s took:
options: 0.717 m, against 0.416 m on the flat
questions.explanation: Downhill a share of gravity pulls the vehicle on while it brakes, so less of the grip is left for stopping.

questions.question: Gravel can be climbed up to about:
questions.explanation: The drive runs out where the tangent of the slope equals the friction less the rolling resistance. For ice the same sum gives 5.1 degrees.

questions.question: Why is a speed limit set on a dry floor not safe on gravel?
options: The stopping distance goes as the inverse of the friction
It is safe if the motors are strong enough
questions.explanation: At 2 m/s the stop was 0.250 m on tarmac and 0.416 m on gravel. A limit chosen for one stopping distance does not give the same on the other.

questions.question: Where two patches overlap, which is under the vehicle?
options: The one with the lower friction
questions.explanation: Patches are laid one over another, so a strip of ice added after a sand pit lies on top of it where they overlap.
